questions.stem: What does the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale test?
questions.why: Three items: facial droop, arm drift, and abnormal speech. Any one abnormal raises stroke probability substantially, which is why it takes under a minute and gets done on every altered patient.

options.t: Pupil size, gag reflex, and grip strength
options.why: Those are cranial nerve and motor checks, not the three items in this scale.

options.t: Orientation to person, place, time, and event
options.why: Orientation is part of a mental status exam rather than a stroke screen.

options.t: Facial droop, arm drift, and speech
Level of consciousness, blood glucose, and gait
options.why: Glucose matters in a suspected stroke, but it is not part of this scale.

questions.stem: Why is last known well time more useful than time of symptom discovery?
questions.why: Thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility is measured from the last moment the patient was known to be at baseline. A patient found down at 0800 who was fine at 2200 has a 10-hour window, not a discovery-time window — that distinction decides what the hospital can offer.

options.t: It determines whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic
options.why: That distinction requires imaging, not a time.

options.t: Symptom discovery is unreliable in an unconscious patient
options.why: It is unreliable, but the reason last known well matters is the treatment clock.

options.t: Insurance requires the exact time of onset be documented
options.why: Documentation follows clinical need; the clock is a treatment question.

options.t: Treatment windows run from when the patient was last normal

questions.stem: Why is a blood glucose check mandatory in any suspected stroke?
questions.why: A low glucose can produce hemiparesis and aphasia that resolve completely with dextrose. It is a treatable stroke mimic, and missing it means transporting a correctable problem as a stroke.

options.t: Thrombolytics cannot be given to a diabetic patient
options.why: Diabetes is not itself a contraindication to thrombolytics.

options.t: The glucose value determines the stroke scale score
options.why: The scale scores physical findings, not laboratory values.

options.t: Hyperglycemia is the most common cause of ischemic stroke
options.why: Hyperglycemia worsens outcomes but is not the cause.

options.t: Hypoglycemia mimics a stroke, focal deficits included

questions.stem: How should blood pressure be managed in a suspected acute ischemic stroke in the field?
questions.why: The brain around an occlusion — the penumbra — depends on that elevated pressure to stay alive. Prehospital blood pressure lowering in ischemic stroke is generally avoided; the decision belongs to the receiving physician.

options.t: Left alone — it is maintaining perfusion
Raised with a fluid bolus to improve cerebral flow
options.why: Routine fluid loading is not the prehospital approach.

options.t: Lowered aggressively to reduce bleeding risk
options.why: Dropping the pressure can extend the ischemic area around the clot.

options.t: Lowered only if the systolic exceeds 140
options.why: That threshold is far below where any intervention would be considered.

questions.stem: What clinical feature most suggests a hemorrhagic rather than ischemic stroke?
questions.why: Sudden severe headache — the worst of the patient's life — with vomiting and rapid decline points toward bleeding. But no field finding is reliable enough to act on: only imaging separates them, which is why every stroke goes to a CT scanner.

options.t: Symptoms that resolved completely within an hour
options.why: Full resolution suggests a transient ischemic attack.

options.t: Abrupt severe headache with rapid deterioration
A history of atrial fibrillation
options.why: Atrial fibrillation is a strong risk factor for embolic ischemic stroke.

options.t: A deficit that came on gradually over an hour
options.why: Gradual onset is more typical of an ischemic event.

questions.stem: A patient's stroke symptoms fully resolved before you arrived. What does that change?
questions.why: A transient ischemic attack means a vessel briefly closed and reopened. A substantial share of these patients stroke within days — the resolved episode is the window to prevent it, not a reason to relax.

options.t: The patient can safely refuse transport once symptoms clear
options.why: Resolution is exactly when a workup is most valuable.

options.t: Nothing — a TIA warns of a coming stroke
The event was not neurologic if the symptoms resolved
options.why: Transient ischemia is a neurologic event by definition.

options.t: Only the deficit that remains needs to be documented
options.why: The resolved deficit is the clinically significant finding.

questions.stem: What defines status epilepticus?
questions.why: Five minutes is the operational threshold, along with back-to-back seizures without regaining consciousness. Past that point the seizure is unlikely to stop on its own and the brain is being injured — it is a true emergency.

options.t: A seizure past 5 minutes, or repeats without recovery
Any seizure in a patient with no seizure history
options.why: A first seizure needs a workup but is not status by definition.

options.t: Two seizures occurring within 24 hours of each other
options.why: Separate seizures with full recovery between them are not status.

options.t: A seizure accompanied by incontinence and tongue biting
options.why: Those are common features of a generalized seizure at any duration.

questions.stem: What is the postictal state, and why does it matter to your assessment?
questions.why: Postictal confusion, drowsiness and gradual clearing are expected. What is not expected is a persistent focal deficit or a patient who fails to improve — that is when you start looking for a head injury, a stroke, or ongoing non-convulsive seizure.

options.t: A seizure that occurs without motor activity
options.why: That describes an absence or a non-convulsive seizure.

options.t: The warning sensation that precedes a seizure
options.why: That is the aura, which comes before rather than after.

options.t: The tonic-clonic phase of the seizure itself
options.why: That is the active seizure.

options.t: The recovery period after a seizure

questions.stem: What should you do first for a patient actively seizing on the floor?
questions.why: Move furniture, pad what you can, position them to protect the airway, and give oxygen. You are managing the environment and the airway, not the seizure itself — most stop within a couple of minutes.

options.t: Move the patient to the stretcher immediately
options.why: Moving a seizing patient is unsafe and unnecessary.

options.t: Place a bite block between the teeth
options.why: Nothing goes in the mouth — it breaks teeth and risks the airway.

options.t: Protect the airway and clear the space
Restrain the limbs to prevent injury
options.why: Restraining a convulsing patient causes fractures and dislocations.

questions.stem: Which cause of a first-time adult seizure is both common and immediately correctable?
questions.why: Check a glucose on every seizure. Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, hyponatremia, toxins, eclampsia, fever and withdrawal all cause seizures and several are correctable — a seizure is a symptom before it is a diagnosis.

options.t: Hypoglycemia
Idiopathic epilepsy
options.why: Idiopathic means no identified cause and no field correction.

options.t: Old traumatic scarring
options.why: Scar tissue is a fixed anatomic cause.

options.t: A brain tumor
options.why: A real cause, but not one correctable in the field.

questions.stem: What does AEIOU-TIPS organize?
questions.why: Alcohol, Epilepsy, Insulin, Overdose, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric, Stroke. Altered mental status has a long differential and most of it is not neurologic — the mnemonic exists so you do not anchor on the first idea.

options.t: The criteria for spinal motion restriction
options.why: Those come from a separate decision rule.

options.t: The components of the Glasgow Coma Scale
options.why: The GCS scores eyes, verbal and motor response.

options.t: The differential for altered mental status
The steps of a neurologic exam
options.why: The exam has its own structure; this mnemonic is a cause list.

questions.stem: What is the lowest possible Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.why: Eyes 1–4, verbal 1–5, motor 1–6. The minimum is 3 and the maximum is 15. A score of 8 or less is the traditional prompt to consider a definitive airway.

options.t: 8, the threshold for airway protection
options.why: 8 is a clinical decision point, not the floor of the scale.

options.t: 1, scored across all three categories combined
options.why: One point is the minimum per category, not overall.

options.t: 0, in a patient with no response at all
options.why: Each of the three components scores a minimum of 1, so zero is impossible.

questions.stem: Which GCS component carries the most prognostic weight?
questions.why: The motor score carries most of the predictive value, and it is the component that survives intubation and language barriers. That is why localizing versus withdrawing versus posturing is worth getting right.

options.t: Eye opening
options.why: Eye opening is the least discriminating of the three.

options.t: Motor response
Verbal response
options.why: Verbal response is easily confounded by intubation or intoxication.

options.t: All three weigh equally in outcome prediction
options.why: The motor score consistently outperforms the others.

questions.stem: What three findings make up Cushing's triad?
questions.why: Hypertension with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and an irregular respiratory pattern. It is a late sign of rising intracranial pressure — the body raising systemic pressure to keep perfusing a compressed brain.

options.t: Falling pressure, rising heart rate, rapid breathing
options.why: That is the pattern of shock, the opposite picture.

options.t: Headache, nausea, and photophobia
options.why: Those are common symptoms of raised pressure but not the triad.

options.t: Distended neck veins, muffled tones, narrow pulse pressure
options.why: That is Beck's triad, which points to cardiac tamponade.

options.t: Rising pressure, falling heart rate, irregular breathing

questions.stem: Why is aggressive hyperventilation avoided in a head-injured patient?
questions.why: Cerebral vessels constrict as CO2 falls. That does briefly lower intracranial pressure — by reducing blood flow to a brain that already needs more. Ventilate to a normal EtCO2 unless herniation is actively occurring.

options.t: It causes a respiratory acidosis that swells the brain
options.why: Hyperventilation produces alkalosis, not acidosis.

options.t: Dropping CO2 constricts cerebral vessels
It raises intracranial pressure by increasing chest pressure
options.why: Intrathoracic pressure has a minor effect compared with the vascular one.

options.t: It has no effect on cerebral blood flow at all
options.why: CO2 is the strongest regulator of cerebral vessel diameter there is.

questions.stem: What does a unilateral blown pupil in a head-injured patient suggest?
questions.why: The oculomotor nerve runs along the path a herniating temporal lobe takes, so it is compressed early. A new fixed dilated pupil with a falling GCS is a neurosurgical emergency.

options.t: A spinal cord injury above the level of T1
options.why: Cord injury does not produce a unilateral fixed dilated pupil.

options.t: Injury to both cerebral hemispheres at once
options.why: Bilateral injury would affect both pupils.

options.t: Herniation compressing cranial nerve three
Direct blunt trauma to the eye itself
options.why: Possible, but a new asymmetric pupil in a deteriorating patient is herniation until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: What separates a primary from a secondary brain injury?
questions.why: You cannot undo the primary injury. Secondary injury — from hypoxia, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperthermia, rising pressure — is what field care exists to prevent. One episode of hypotension measurably worsens outcome.

options.t: Primary is the concussion; secondary is the skull fracture
options.why: Both fractures and concussions occur at the moment of impact.

options.t: Primary is treated in the field; secondary at the hospital
options.why: Preventing secondary injury is exactly what field care is for.

options.t: Primary is at impact; secondary develops after
Primary is closed injury; secondary is penetrating
options.why: That distinction is about mechanism, not timing.

questions.stem: Which single physiologic derangement most worsens outcome after a traumatic brain injury?
questions.why: The injured brain has lost its ability to autoregulate, so cerebral perfusion follows systemic pressure directly. A single documented episode of hypotension roughly doubles mortality — keeping the pressure up is the intervention.

options.t: Mild hyperglycemia
options.why: Elevated glucose is associated with worse outcomes but far less powerfully.

options.t: Hypotension
A brief episode of tachycardia
options.why: Tachycardia is a compensatory response rather than a driver of injury.

options.t: A single vomiting episode
options.why: Vomiting matters for airway protection, not as an independent outcome driver.

questions.stem: Which headache description is most concerning for subarachnoid hemorrhage?
questions.why: A headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds — often described as being hit in the head — is a subarachnoid bleed until imaging says otherwise. Onset speed matters more than severity.

options.t: Sudden and maximal at onset — a thunderclap
Behind one eye, waking the patient at the same hour nightly
options.why: That pattern suggests cluster headache.

options.t: Throbbing, one-sided, with nausea and light sensitivity
options.why: That pattern fits migraine.

options.t: A band-like pressure that built through the day
options.why: That description suits a tension headache.

questions.stem: A trauma patient is hypotensive with a heart rate of 52 and warm, dry, pink skin. What should you suspect?
questions.why: Losing sympathetic outflow leaves vessels dilated and the heart unable to speed up. Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin is the opposite of every other shock — and hemorrhage still has to be ruled out alongside it.

options.t: Neurogenic shock from a spinal cord injury
Hemorrhagic shock from an unrecognized bleed
options.why: Hemorrhage produces tachycardia with cool, pale skin.

options.t: Septic shock from a pre-existing infection
options.why: Sepsis in a trauma patient is unlikely at the time of injury.

options.t: Cardiogenic shock from blunt cardiac injury
options.why: Cardiogenic shock presents with cool, clammy skin and signs of congestion.

questions.stem: What separates spinal shock from neurogenic shock?
questions.why: Spinal shock is the temporary loss of cord function below an injury — flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes. Neurogenic shock is the hemodynamic consequence of losing sympathetic tone. One is neurologic, the other circulatory.

options.t: Spinal shock affects only the legs; neurogenic the whole body
options.why: Neither is defined by which limbs are involved.

options.t: Spinal shock is neurologic; neurogenic shock is circulatory
Spinal shock is permanent; neurogenic shock is temporary
options.why: Spinal shock is often the temporary one.

options.t: They are two names for the same condition
options.why: They describe different problems that frequently occur together.

questions.stem: Why should a stroke patient's deficits be documented in specific terms rather than as 'weak on one side'?
questions.why: Whether a deficit is improving or extending changes management, and that comparison is impossible without a specific starting description. "Left arm drifts to the bed in 5 seconds, unable to name a pen" is usable; "weak on the left" is not.

options.t: Specific wording is needed to score the Cincinnati scale
options.why: The scale is scored from three findings, not from narrative detail.

options.t: Detailed documentation is required for billing purposes
options.why: Billing is not why the detail matters clinically.

options.t: It gives the hospital a baseline to measure against
The deficit pattern determines the transport priority
options.why: Priority is high for any acute stroke regardless of pattern.

questions.stem: What is the single most valuable thing you can do for a large-vessel stroke patient?
questions.why: Everything in stroke care is time to reperfusion. Pre-notification lets the hospital assemble the team and clear the scanner before arrival, and the last known well time decides which treatments are still on the table.

options.t: Position the patient fully upright for the whole transport
options.why: Positioning is a comfort and airway decision, not the priority.

options.t: Give aspirin to limit clot growth
options.why: Aspirin is withheld until a bleed has been ruled out by imaging.

options.t: Establish two large-bore IVs before departing
options.why: Access is useful but it does not shorten time to reperfusion.

options.t: Notify the stroke center early with a last known well time

questions.stem: Match each stroke finding to what it suggests about the location.
questions.why: Language sits in the left hemisphere for most people, so aphasia with right-sided weakness localizes left. Posterior circulation strokes present with the Ds — dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia — and are the ones most often missed.
pairs: Deficit resolving completely within an hour
Deficit present on waking, unclear onset

questions.stem: An elderly patient is newly confused with a low-grade fever and no focal deficit. What is high on the list?
questions.why: In older patients, infection frequently presents as confusion before it presents as fever or pain — urinary infections and pneumonia especially. Acute confusion in an elder is delirium until proven otherwise, and delirium has a cause.

options.t: A subdural hematoma from remote trauma
options.why: Worth considering, but the fever points elsewhere first.

options.t: An acute ischemic stroke
options.why: Stroke usually produces a focal deficit rather than global confusion.

options.t: New-onset dementia developing over hours
options.why: Dementia develops over months and years, not hours.

options.t: Infection, commonly urinary

questions.stem: A pregnant patient in the third trimester has a first-time seizure. What must you consider?
questions.why: A seizure in the second half of pregnancy or shortly after delivery is eclampsia until shown otherwise. It is a hypertensive emergency of pregnancy, magnesium is the treatment, and the definitive fix is delivery.

options.t: Eclampsia
Hypoglycemia from pregnancy-related fasting
options.why: Worth checking, but it does not carry eclampsia's urgency.

options.t: A febrile seizure, as occurs in children
options.why: Febrile seizures are a pediatric phenomenon.

options.t: A new epilepsy diagnosis unrelated to the pregnancy
options.why: New epilepsy is possible but eclampsia is the time-critical concern.
